Yikes
YYKS
interjection (Gen Alpha slang)
An American interjection of alarm, dismay, or embarrassment, in use by the mid-twentieth century, sometimes said to be an alteration of yoicks, the old English fox-hunting cry. Long a cartoon word, it was revived online in the 2010s, with the intensified "big yikes" (c. 2019) for something deeply embarrassing; Gen Alpha uses "yikes" for awkward moments, bad news, and cringe.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

"Yikes!" is what you say when something is embarrassing or alarming — a bad grade, a spill, an awkward moment. "Big yikes" means very embarrassing. The Christian observation: the Bible is full of yikes moments, and they tell the story of the gospel. The very first one came in the garden: "I was afraid, because I was naked; and I hid myself" (Gen 3:10). When Isaiah saw the holiness of God, he said the biggest yikes of all: "Woe is me! for I am undone; because I am a man of unclean lips" (Isa 6:5). When Peter saw Jesus’s power, he fell down and said, "Depart from me; for I am a sinful man, O Lord" (Luk 5:8). Every one of those moments was met by mercy: God clothed Adam, an angel touched Isaiah’s lips with a coal and said "thy sin purged," and Jesus told Peter, "Fear not." The deepest yikes is answered by the best news: "There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus" (Rom 8:1). A father can tell a five-year-old: "When we do something wrong, we might feel ‘yikes!’ inside. But God doesn’t make us hide. When we say sorry, He forgives us — that’s what Jesus came to do."

Webster 1828 Definition

American interjection of alarm or embarrassment (mid-20th c.; "big yikes," c. 2019) — the small shame-cry that Scripture’s great yikes moments, from Eden to Isaiah to Peter, show God answering with mercy.

YIKES, interj. (American English, mid-20th c.; revived online 2010s; Gen Alpha) An exclamation of alarm, dismay, or embarrassment. "Yikes, I forgot my homework."

Big yikes (c. 2019) — something very embarrassing.

Possibly from yoicks, a fox-hunting cry.

Decode for parents: harmless; a ready doorway to talk about shame and grace.

Key Scripture

Gen 3:10 — "And he said, I heard thy voice in the garden, and I was afraid, because I was naked; and I hid myself."

Isa 6:5 — "Then said I, Woe is me! for I am undone; because I am a man of unclean lips, and I dwell in the midst of a people of unclean lips: for mine eyes have seen the King, the LORD of hosts."

Luk 5:8 — "When Simon Peter saw it, he fell down at Jesus' knees, saying, Depart from me; for I am a sinful man, O Lord."

Rom 8:1 — "There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus, who walk not after the flesh, but after the Spirit."

Modern Corruption

"Yikes" is a harmless cry of embarrassment; Scripture’s own yikes moments show the shame of sinners and the mercy that answers it.

expand to see more

There is nothing to correct in the word. If anything deserves care, it is the culture of cringe that "big yikes" belongs to — the habit of calling out other people’s embarrassing moments. A child who says "big yikes" at a classmate’s mistake is close to mockery.

Use it as a doorway. Every child knows the yikes feeling of shame. Tell her about Adam hiding, Isaiah undone, and Peter on his knees — and about the God who came looking, cleansed, and said "fear not." A child who knows that shame meets mercy will hide less and confess more.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Perhaps yoicks (fox-hunting cry) → American yikes (mid-20th c.) → online revival and "big yikes" (2010s).

"No condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus — the end of every yikes (Rom 8:1)."
